discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) that made robust femtosecond lasers possible
motivation: Modern ultrafast science rests on a small number of enabling inventions. Moulton's titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982-86) gave a broadband gain medium that can support pulses of a few optical cycles. Sibbett's group discovered self-mode-locking in Ti:sapphire in 1991, now understood as Kerr-lens mode-locking. This turned difficult dye-laser systems into simple, reliable femtosecond sources. Keller's semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) made passive mode-locking self-starting and usable across solid-state, fiber and semiconductor lasers. Together these advances make up the oscillator front end of nearly every chirped-pulse amplifier, attosecond source and frequency comb. They underpin Nobel-recognised work in femtochemistry, frequency metrology, high-field physics and attosecond science, as well as multiphoton microscopy and laser surgery. The inventions themselves have never been recognised. These are simple, clever ideas that removed a barrier and opened an entire field.
